docs.title: Positive Comments
docs.text: Voice of the Customer Restated Customer Need "TLDR: This is a great kit, very affordable, follow the online PDF as it did not come with instructions in the box. The programming part is straight forward to get it running. simply clone the repo and run setup script. Have fun! I got this RaspClaws kit for my kids as a Christmas present, and couldn’t be happier. It’s is a great start for anyone trying to get started playing with robotics. The price is fairly reasonable given the parts that it comes with, Picam, servos x15 +1 one extra, Accelerometer, LEDs, ect. Once assembled, it is fairly compact and even looks pretty cool. There were no instructions in the box, but instructions could be found on the link provided on the product page of amazon. The assembly process is straight forward simply follow the instructions and you’ll be setup in no time. Overall, it took me less than a day to put it all together. Everything is OpenSource, so you simply have to download the code from their Git repo, and run the setup.py. The setup script will take care of installing everything needed for the RaspClaws to work. Once everything was setup and installed, I was able to run the RaspClaws.py without any issues and connected successfully to the ‘spider’, and It crawls … it’s creepy. Overall, this is a great learning/fun kit! I look forward to see how they play with it longterm. P.S: you may want a second sets of batteries, to limit your play downtime :-D" 1. docs.title: Project Objective
docs.text:
This project aims to create a robotic leg that can be easily understood and leveraged so that other robotic enthusiasts can adapt and utilize this leg in their own systems and creations.

One of our goals is to create a leg that is easy to use, tweak, and modify from the original design. Users could purchase the physical leg to avoid building and wiring it themselves, or access the software and design files to modify the leg for their own projects.

Back to Table of Contents

docs.title: Stakeholders
docs.text:
• Target Group: Robotics enthusiasts of all ages looking to adapt existing systems into larger projects and products.
  • Target Purchaser: Individuals, schools, or businesses looking to create or modify walking or crawling robotic systems.
  • Customer Service: Prefers easy-to-repair, recyclable products and straightforward solutions to customer complaints.
  • Marketing & Sales Division: Looks for unique selling points that can attract potential customers.
  • Retailers: Prefer products that can withstand different storage conditions, including changes in temperature, vibration, humidity, and atmospheric pressure, with strong and compact packaging.

Back to Table of Contents

docs.title: User Story 1: Buzz Lightyear
docs.text:
Goal: Create a multi-legged prop for a live-action film scene.

Scenario:

Buzz Lightyear is a prop master working on an upcoming horror film. He needs to control eight spider legs, so he purchases eight robotic legs and uses a custom setup rather than a mobile phone application.

Using the open API and Bluetooth control interface, Buzz bypasses the standard companion application and writes a custom script to synchronize the legs with the other components of the prop.

docs.title: User Story 2: John Doe
docs.text:
Goal: Build a custom quadruped or hexapod crawler without designing mechanical limbs from scratch.

Scenario:

John Doe is a 22-year-old working on a custom spider robot project. He purchases four assembled robotic legs so he can begin working on quadruped movement.

During testing, one of the structural links breaks. Because the leg uses off-the-shelf fasteners, PLA/PETG 3D-printed parts, and non-proprietary mechanical components, John can print a replacement part and install it using standard tools.

Back to Table of Contents

docs.title: Design Aspects
docs.text: The product requirements use a priority scale from P1 (lowest priority) to P10 (highest priority).

docs.title: Hardware/Product Design
docs.text:
• 1.1 The leg shall be constructed primarily from 3D-printed structural components to enable rapid iteration and low-cost design changes. (P10)
  • 1.2 The leg shall use standard metal fasteners instead of adhesives or welds for joint assembly, allowing components to be disassembled and replaced without specialized tools. (P9)
  • 1.3 The leg's structural components shall be printable using commonly available thermoplastics, such as PLA and PETG. (P8)
  • 1.4 The leg's housing and joints shall be designed for disassembly using standard tools and removable fasteners. (P8)
  • 1.5 The leg's printed components shall use single-material construction where possible to support recyclability. (P6)

docs.title: Software/Functionality
docs.text:
• 2.1 The leg's control software shall be written in Python to maximize accessibility for hobbyist and student developers. (P10)
  • 2.2 The leg shall use industry-standard communication protocols, including UART and I2C, for sensor and actuator communication. (P9)
  • 2.3 The leg's software shall be modular, separating motion control, sensor input, and communication functions. (P8)
  • 2.4 The codebase shall include documentation and a setup guide allowing a first-time user to run a basic movement demonstration within one hour. (P7)

docs.title: Interactivity
docs.text:
• 3.1 The leg shall support wireless control through Bluetooth using a companion smartphone application as its primary user interaction method. (P10)
  • 3.2 The control interface shall provide an open API or command set so users can create alternative control methods, such as gamepads, voice commands, or autonomous scripts. (P8)
  • 3.3 The companion application shall provide diagnostic information, including connection status, battery level, and joint position. (P7)

docs.title: Customization
docs.text:
• 4.1 The leg's software and firmware shall be released under an open-source license to allow user modification. (P10)
  • 4.2 The hardware design files, including CAD models and wiring diagrams, shall be publicly available. (P9)
  • 4.3 The leg shall use a standardized hardware configuration while allowing users to modify components after purchase. (P7)
  • 4.4 The design shall use commonly available off-the-shelf fasteners and connectors to simplify replacement and upgrades. (P8)

docs.title: Manufacturing
docs.text:
• 5.1 The leg's body shall be manufactured using 3D-printed components to reduce tooling costs and allow design revisions. (P10)
  • 5.2 Electronic and mechanical components, including motors, fasteners, and bearings, shall be sourced as off-the-shelf parts. (P9)
  • 5.3 Packaging shall withstand changes in temperature, humidity, vibration, and atmospheric pressure during normal shipping and storage. (P8)
  • 5.4 Packaging shall be tamper-evident and resistant to theft and vandalism. (P7)
  • 5.5 Packaging materials shall be recyclable or reusable where possible. (P5)

docs.title: Safety
docs.text:
• 6.1 The leg's actuators shall include current-limiting or stall-detection safeguards to prevent motor damage and reduce injury risks. (P10)
  • 6.2 Exposed moving joints shall include guards or shields to reduce pinch-point risks. (P9)
  • 6.3 The electrical system shall include over-voltage and over-current protection. (P9)
  • 6.4 The software shall include a fail-safe stop state to prevent uncontrolled movement if communication is lost. (P9)
  • 6.5 The leg's materials shall be non-toxic and free of sharp edges. (P7)

Back to Table of Contents

docs.title: Requirement Criteria Specifications
docs.text:
The following criteria describe how the team will verify that each product requirement has been met.

Verification methods include inspection, analysis, testing, and demonstration.

Requirement Requirement Criteria Specification Verification Method 1.1 At least 75% of custom structural components, by part count, shall be 3D printed. Inspection 1.2 Structural joints shall use removable metal fasteners and be disassembled using standard hand tools. Inspection / Demonstration 1.3 Custom structural components shall be printable using PLA or PETG filament. Inspection / Demonstration 1.4 A designated structural link shall be removable and reinstalled within 20 minutes. Demonstration 1.5 Printed structural components shall use a single identified thermoplastic material where possible. Inspection 2.1 The primary control software shall be written in Python and execute a basic movement command. Inspection / Demonstration 2.2 UART and I2C communication interfaces shall successfully transmit sensor and actuator data during 10 consecutive trials. Test 2.3 Motion control, sensor input, and communication functions shall exist as separate software modules. Inspection 2.4 A first-time user shall complete a basic movement demonstration within 60 minutes using the documentation. Demonstration 3.1 The leg shall connect to a companion smartphone application through Bluetooth and execute a movement command. Demonstration 3.2 The documented API or command set shall accept movement commands from an alternative control method. Demonstration 3.3 The companion application shall display connection status, battery level, and joint-position information. Demonstration 4.1 The software repository shall contain an open-source license and accessible source files. Inspection 4.2 CAD models and wiring diagrams shall be available in the published documentation. Inspection 4.3 The completed leg shall use a documented standard hardware configuration while allowing component replacement. Inspection / Demonstration 4.4 Fasteners and connectors shall be commercially available and non-proprietary. Inspection 5.1 Custom body components designated for additive manufacturing shall be 3D printed. Inspection 5.2 Electronic and mechanical components shall have commercially available replacements or documented equivalents. Inspection 5.3 The packaged leg shall remain functional and show no structural damage following defined shipping-condition tests. Test 5.4 Packaging shall include a tamper-evident feature. Inspection / Demonstration 5.5 Packaging materials shall be identified as recyclable or reusable where feasible. Inspection 6.1 Current-limiting or stall-detection safeguards shall activate during controlled testing before an actuator exceeds its rated limits. Test 6.2 Accessible pinch points shall include physical guards or shields. Inspection 6.3 The power system shall include appropriate over-voltage and over-current protection. Inspection / Analysis 6.4 Disconnecting Bluetooth during movement shall trigger the fail-safe state and stop commanded movement. Test 6.5 Manufactured surfaces shall be inspected for sharp edges, and materials shall be documented as non-toxic for their intended use. Inspection

docs.title: Team Block Diagram
docs.text:
Our team is designing one robotic leg that could eventually be used as part of a six-legged spider robot.

The leg is divided into four subsystems, with each teammate responsible for one PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano microcontroller.

We are using a hub-and-spoke layout, meaning Preston's Nano acts as the main controller while the other three Nanos connect directly to it.

Preston's Nano will handle leg kinematics and movement coordination. The other Nanos will control their assigned motors, actuators, and sensors.

docs.title: Original Team 102 Block Diagram
docs.text:
Figure 1: Original Team 102 block diagram showing Preston's main controller connected to Akshan's servo motor, Bex's linear actuator and pressure sensor, and Kaushik's linear actuator and IMU.

Download the editable draw.io file

This diagram shows our original subsystem layout and the 8-pin ribbon cable connections between the four boards.

As the project develops, we will update the electrical connections and software communication to match our final hardware choices.

Back to Table of Contents

docs.title: Subsystem Responsibilities
docs.text:
Each teammate is responsible for developing and testing the software and hardware for their assigned subsystem.

Teammate Controller Responsibilities Preston Potts Main Processor Nano Leg kinematics, IR remote input, movement coordination, UART communication, and global status Akshan Bhelkar Driver Nano 1 Servo motor control, joint limit monitoring, and proposed diagnostic display Bex Baker Driver Nano 2 Linear actuator A, pressure sensor, joint limit switches, and joint status Kaushik Gunasekaren Driver Nano 3 Linear actuator B, IMU, joint limit switches, and joint status

docs.title: Main Processor Nano - Preston
docs.text:
Preston's Nano will be responsible for coordinating the overall movement of the robotic leg.

It will:

  • Receive commands from an IR remote.
  • Calculate the required joint positions.
  • Send movement commands to the other Nanos.
  • Receive feedback from the joint controllers.
  • Monitor the overall system status.
  • Send stop commands when a fault is detected.

docs.title: Driver Nano 1 - Akshan
docs.text:
Akshan's Nano will control the servo motor.

It will:

  • Receive servo position commands.
  • Generate the servo control signal.
  • Monitor the joint's limit switches.
  • Send status information to Preston's Nano.
  • Support the proposed diagnostic display.

The display model and programming details are still TBD.

docs.title: Driver Nano 2 - Bex
docs.text:
Bex's Nano will control Linear Actuator A and read the pressure sensor.

It will:

  • Receive movement commands.
  • Control the linear actuator through a motor driver.
  • Read pressure sensor information.
  • Monitor two limit switches.
  • Send feedback to Preston's Nano.
  • Control the joint status indicator.

docs.title: Driver Nano 3 - Kaushik
docs.text:
Kaushik's Nano will control Linear Actuator B and read the IMU.

It will:

  • Receive movement commands.
  • Control the linear actuator through a motor driver.
  • Read IMU measurements.
  • Monitor two limit switches.
  • Send feedback to Preston's Nano.
  • Control the joint status indicator.

Back to Table of Contents

docs.title: Connection Layout
docs.text:
Our team plans to connect the four Nanos using 8-pin ribbon cables.

Each spoke Nano connects directly to Preston's main controller.

docs.title: Hub Connections
docs.text:
Hub Connector Connected Nano Purpose Connector 1 Akshan Servo commands and feedback Connector 2 Bex Linear actuator A commands and pressure feedback Connector 3 Kaushik Linear actuator B commands and IMU feedback

The original class-standard connector layout uses:

  • Pins 1-5 for digital signals.
  • Pins 6-7 for analog signals.
  • Pin 8 for ground.

docs.title: Proposed Ribbon Cable Pin Assignments
docs.text:
Pin Type Akshan Bex Kaushik 1 Digital UART TX UART TX UART TX 2 Digital UART RX UART RX UART RX 3 Digital Reserved Reserved Reserved 4 Digital Reserved Reserved Reserved 5 Digital Reserved Reserved Reserved 6 Analog Reserved Reserved Reserved 7 Analog Reserved Reserved Reserved 8 Ground Common ground Common ground Common ground

Note: These are proposed signal assignments, not finalized wiring. The TX and RX directions must be verified for both ends of each cable.

The exact microcontroller pin assignments will be finalized when the electrical schematics are completed.

Back to Table of Contents

docs.title: Hardware and Sensors
docs.text: Our robotic leg will use three motorized joints controlled by the four Nanos.

docs.title: Planned Hardware
docs.text: Component Assigned Nano Purpose IR receiver Preston Receive commands from a TV remote RGB/status LED Preston Display overall system status Servo motor Akshan Control one joint Diagnostic display Akshan Display system information Linear actuator A Bex Control one joint Pressure sensor Bex Detect pressure or contact Linear actuator B Kaushik Control one joint IMU Kaushik Measure motion and orientation Limit switches Joint controllers Detect joint travel limits White LED Joint controllers Display joint status

docs.title: Limit Switches
docs.text:
Our current plan includes two limit switches for each joint.

Since the leg has three joints, we plan to use six limit switches total.

The switches will help prevent the joints from moving beyond their allowed mechanical range.

docs.title: Pressure Sensor
docs.text:
The pressure sensor will be connected to Bex's Nano.

It will help detect contact or pressure at the robotic leg.

The final sensor location and pressure thresholds have not been determined.

docs.title: IMU
docs.text:
The IMU will be connected to Kaushik's Nano.

It will provide information about the leg's movement and orientation.

The exact IMU model and communication interface are still TBD.

Back to Table of Contents

docs.title: Process Diagram
docs.text:
The software for the robotic leg will be divided among the four Nanos.

The main controller will calculate the movement commands, while the other three controllers will operate their assigned hardware.

The complete software flow diagram is included on our Software Proposal page.

docs.title: Main Controller Process
docs.text:
1. Initialize the Nano.
  2. Initialize communication.
  3. Initialize the IR receiver and indicator lights.
  4. Wait for a user command.
  5. Read the IR remote input.
  6. Calculate the required joint positions.
  7. Send commands to the three driver Nanos.
  8. Receive sensor and joint feedback.
  9. Check for faults or stop commands.
  10. Update the global status indicator.
  11. Repeat the process.

docs.title: Joint Controller Process
docs.text:
1. Initialize the Nano.
  2. Initialize communication.
  3. Initialize the assigned actuator and sensors.
  4. Wait for a movement command.
  5. Check the command and joint limits.
  6. Control the assigned motor or actuator.
  7. Read sensor information.
  8. Monitor for faults.
  9. Send feedback to the main Nano.
  10. Repeat the process.

Each driver Nano will operate independently while communicating with the main controller.

Back to Table of Contents

docs.title: UART Communication
docs.text:
Our current communication plan is to use UART between the four Nanos.

Preston's main Nano will communicate with each of the three driver Nanos through a separate connection.

docs.title: Communication Layout
docs.text:
Connection Commands Feedback Preston to Akshan Servo target position Servo status and limit information Preston to Bex Linear actuator A command Pressure sensor and limit information Preston to Kaushik Linear actuator B command IMU and limit information

Each UART connection requires:

  • TX (transmit)
  • RX (receive)
  • Common ground

The TX signal from one Nano connects to the RX signal on the other Nano.

The final UART channels, pin assignments, baud rate, and communication settings still need to be verified.

Back to Table of Contents

docs.title: Message Structure
docs.text:
The Nanos will need a consistent message format so they can send and receive commands correctly.

The following message structure is our current proposal.

docs.title: Command Message
docs.text: Field Purpose Start Identifies the beginning of a message Destination Identifies the receiving Nano Command Identifies the requested action Target Position Contains the requested joint position Sequence Number Identifies the command Error Check Helps detect communication errors

docs.title: Feedback Message
docs.text: Field Purpose Start Identifies the beginning of a message Source Identifies the sending Nano Joint Status Reports the joint's operating state Sensor Data Contains pressure or IMU information Limit Status Reports limit switch activity Fault Status Reports detected errors Error Check Helps detect communication errors

docs.title: Proposed Command Types
docs.text: Command Description MOVE Move a joint toward a requested position STOP Stop commanded joint movement STATUS Request current controller status HOME Start an approved joint homing procedure RESET Clear an eligible fault after safety checks

docs.title: Proposed Feedback Types
docs.text:
Feedback Description READY Controller is initialized MOVING Joint is moving POSITION Reports position information SENSOR Reports sensor measurements LIMIT A joint limit is active FAULT A fault has been detected STOPPED Joint movement has stopped

These message types are proposals. The exact encoding, field sizes, and error-checking method still need to be finalized.

docs.title: Indicator Lights
docs.text:
Our team plans to use different colored LEDs to indicate the status of the robotic leg.

LED Color Purpose Yellow Power indicator Green Board power indicator Blue Global status indicator White Joint status indicator

docs.title: Yellow LED
docs.text: The yellow LED indicates that power is present.

docs.title: Green LED
docs.text: The green LED indicates that the board is receiving power.

docs.title: Blue LED
docs.text: The blue LED will indicate the overall status of the robotic leg.

docs.title: White LED
docs.text:
The white LED will indicate the status of an individual joint.

The exact behavior of the blue and white LEDs will be determined during software development.

docs.title: Power Distribution
docs.text:
Our team would prefer to use an external 12V DC power supply rather than relying on a computer USB connection.

However, the final power supply has not been selected.

Some early schematics show a 9V power source as a placeholder. This is not the confirmed power source for the final design.

docs.title: Proposed Power Arrangement
docs.text:
1. An external DC supply provides power to the robotic leg.
  2. Power distribution circuitry supplies the individual subsystems.
  3. Voltage regulators provide the correct voltage for the Nanos and sensors.
  4. Motor drivers receive the voltage required by the selected actuators.
  5. The controllers share a common ground reference.

The final supply voltage, current requirements, voltage regulators, and protection components will be determined after the actuator models are selected.

Power Supply Status: TBD

Back to Table of Contents

docs.title: Safety and Fault Handling
docs.text: Our team plans to include several safety features in the robotic leg.

docs.title: Joint Limit Protection
docs.text:
Each joint controller will monitor its two limit switches.

If a limit switch is activated, the controller will prevent further movement in the restricted direction.

docs.title: Communication Loss
docs.text:
If a Nano stops receiving valid commands for longer than the selected timeout, it should enter a safe state.

The affected joint should stop commanded movement until communication is restored and the controller is ready.

docs.title: Invalid Commands
docs.text:
Each controller should check incoming commands before moving its actuator.

Commands outside the allowed range should be rejected or limited.

docs.title: Fault Reporting
docs.text:
The joint controllers should send fault information to Preston's Nano.

Possible faults include:

  • Communication loss
  • Joint limit reached
  • Invalid movement command
  • Sensor failure
  • Motor stall or overload
  • Position feedback failure

The exact response to each fault will depend on the selected hardware.

Back to Table of Contents

docs.title: Minimizing Interconnections
docs.text:
Using a hub-and-spoke layout allows each Nano to communicate directly with Preston's main controller.

UART communication can reduce the number of individual control and sensor signals that need to travel between boards.

Each driver Nano will process its own sensor readings and control its assigned actuator.

docs.title: Why Hub and Spoke?
docs.text:
The robotic leg has three joints that need to work together.

Preston's Nano will calculate the required movement for all three joints and send commands to the driver Nanos.

This allows the main controller to focus on movement coordination while the other Nanos handle their local hardware.

docs.title: Independent Joint Control
docs.text:
The three driver Nanos will be able to operate independently.

Each Nano can receive commands, move its assigned actuator, monitor sensors, and return feedback without waiting for another joint to finish unless synchronization is required.

docs.title: Risk of Losing a Controller
docs.text:
Preston's Nano is the central controller, making it an important part of the system.

If the main controller fails, coordinated movement cannot continue.

If one driver Nano fails, the affected joint will no longer be controlled correctly.

The team should make sure the system enters a safe state when communication or controller failures occur.

Keeping the software modular and documented will also make it easier to replace a controller if needed.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Our team is developing the software for one robotic spider leg that could eventually be used as part of a six-legged robot.

The leg will use four PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano microcontrollers. Each teammate is responsible for programming a different part of the system.

Instead of having one Nano control everything, we are dividing the work between a main controller and three driver controllers.

Preston's Nano will calculate the leg kinematics and coordinate movement. The other three Nanos will control their assigned motors, actuators, and sensors.

Our goal is to make the software modular so each teammate can develop and test their part before combining everything into one working robotic leg.

Back to Table of Contents

docs.title: Software Objectives
docs.text:
The main goals of our software are:

  1. Control three joints of one robotic leg.
  2. Calculate the joint positions required for movement.
  3. Receive user commands through an IR remote.
  4. Communicate between four Nanos using UART.
  5. Control one servo motor and two linear actuators.
  6. Read pressure sensor and IMU information.
  7. Monitor limit switches at each joint.
  8. Use indicator lights to display system and joint status.
  9. Stop commanded movement when a fault occurs.
  10. Allow each controller to be programmed and tested separately.

Back to Table of Contents

docs.title: Software Architecture Diagram
docs.text:
The following block diagram shows our proposed software and hardware arrangement.

Preston's Nano is the main processor. It calculates the required joint positions and sends commands to the three driver Nanos.

Each driver Nano controls its assigned hardware and returns feedback to the main controller.

Figure 1: Proposed leg control block diagram showing the four Nanos, actuators, sensors, and main controller.

docs.title: Architecture Overview
docs.text:
Controller Teammate Responsibilities Main Processor Nano Preston Potts Kinematics, IR remote, movement coordination, and global status Driver Nano 1 Akshan Bhelkar Servo motor and proposed diagnostic display Driver Nano 2 Bex Baker Linear Actuator A and pressure sensor Driver Nano 3 Kaushik Gunasekaren Linear Actuator B and IMU

The current communication plan uses UART between the Nanos.

Note: The diagram was created during our earlier design planning and labels some connections as I2C/Serial. Our current plan is to use UART for communication between the Nanos. The final hardware connections still need to be verified.

Back to Table of Contents

docs.title: Software Flow Diagram
docs.text:
The software flow diagram shows the proposed operating process for all four Nanos.

The main controller receives commands, calculates joint positions, sends movement instructions, and checks feedback.

The three driver Nanos receive commands, operate their assigned hardware, read sensor information, and report their status.

Figure 2: Proposed software flow diagram showing the main processor and three driver controllers.

docs.title: Main Software Process
docs.text:
1. Initialize the main Nano.
  2. Initialize communication and indicator lights.
  3. Initialize the IR receiver.
  4. Wait for a command from the remote.
  5. Read the requested movement.
  6. Calculate the required joint positions.
  7. Send commands to the driver Nanos.
  8. Receive sensor and joint feedback.
  9. Check for faults or stop commands.
  10. Update the system status indicator.
  11. Repeat the process.

docs.title: Driver Nano Process
docs.text:
1. Initialize the Nano.
  2. Initialize UART communication.
  3. Initialize the assigned actuator and sensors.
  4. Wait for a movement command.
  5. Check the command and joint limits.
  6. Operate the assigned actuator.
  7. Read sensor information.
  8. Check for faults.
  9. Send feedback to the main Nano.
  10. Repeat the process.

Each driver Nano will run its own control loop while communicating with Preston's main controller.

Back to Table of Contents

docs.title: Subsystem Responsibilities
docs.text:
Our software is divided into four subsystems.

Each teammate will be responsible for programming, testing, and documenting their assigned controller.

Function Responsible Teammate IR remote input Preston Leg kinematics Preston Movement coordination Preston Global status indicator Preston Servo motor control Akshan Diagnostic display Akshan - TBD Linear Actuator A Bex Pressure sensor Bex Linear Actuator B Kaushik IMU Kaushik Limit switch monitoring Each joint controller UART communication All four controllers Fault handling All four controllers

Back to Table of Contents

docs.title: Main Controller - Preston
docs.text:
Preston's Nano will act as the main processor for the robotic leg.

It will receive input from the IR remote, calculate the required joint positions, and send movement commands to the other controllers.

docs.title: Planned Functions
docs.text:
• Initialize the system.
  • Read IR remote commands.
  • Calculate leg kinematics.
  • Send movement commands.
  • Receive sensor feedback.
  • Monitor communication.
  • Update the global indicator.
  • Handle faults and stop commands.

The main controller will coordinate movement but will not directly operate every actuator.

Back to Table of Contents

docs.title: Servo Controller - Akshan
docs.text:
Akshan's Nano will control the servo motor assigned to one of the leg joints.

It will receive target position commands from Preston's Nano and generate the appropriate servo control signal.

docs.title: Planned Functions
docs.text:
1. Initialize the servo interface.
  2. Initialize UART communication.
  3. Monitor the joint limit switches.
  4. Receive the target position.
  5. Check whether the movement is allowed.
  6. Control the servo.
  7. Monitor joint status.
  8. Send feedback to Preston's Nano.

Akshan's Nano is also assigned the proposed diagnostic display.

The display model, wiring, and software are still TBD.

Back to Table of Contents

docs.title: Linear Actuator A - Bex
docs.text:
Bex's Nano will control Linear Actuator A and monitor the pressure sensor.

It will receive movement commands from Preston's Nano and operate the actuator through its motor driver.

docs.title: Planned Functions
docs.text:
1. Initialize UART communication.
  2. Initialize the motor driver interface.
  3. Initialize the pressure sensor.
  4. Initialize two limit switches.
  5. Wait for a movement command.
  6. Check whether movement is allowed.
  7. Extend, retract, or stop the actuator.
  8. Read the pressure sensor.
  9. Monitor the limit switches.
  10. Send sensor and joint status information to Preston's Nano.
  11. Update the joint indicator.

docs.title: Inputs and Outputs
docs.text:
Type Component Purpose Input UART RX Receive movement commands Input Pressure sensor Detect pressure or contact Input Limit switch 1 Detect one travel limit Input Limit switch 2 Detect the opposite travel limit Output Motor driver signals Control actuator movement Output UART TX Send feedback Output White LED Display joint status

The final actuator model, motor driver, and pin assignments are still TBD.

Back to Table of Contents

docs.title: Linear Actuator B - Kaushik
docs.text:
Kaushik's Nano will control Linear Actuator B and collect information from the IMU.

The IMU will provide measurements that can be used to monitor the movement and orientation of the robotic leg.

docs.title: Planned Functions
docs.text:
1. Initialize UART communication.
  2. Initialize the motor driver interface.
  3. Initialize the IMU.
  4. Initialize two limit switches.
  5. Wait for a movement command.
  6. Check the joint limits.
  7. Control Linear Actuator B.
  8. Read IMU measurements.
  9. Monitor for faults.
  10. Send feedback to Preston's Nano.
  11. Update the joint indicator.

The final actuator model, IMU, motor driver, and pin assignments are still TBD.

Back to Table of Contents

docs.title: UART Communication
docs.text:
Our current plan is to use UART communication between the four Nanos.

Preston's main Nano will communicate directly with each driver Nano through a separate connection.

docs.title: Communication Layout
docs.text:
Connection Commands Sent Feedback Returned Preston to Akshan Servo target position Servo and joint status Preston to Bex Actuator A movement command Pressure and limit information Preston to Kaushik Actuator B movement command IMU and limit information

Each UART connection requires:

  • TX (transmit)
  • RX (receive)
  • Common ground

The TX signal from one Nano connects to the RX signal on the other Nano.

docs.title: Proposed Commands
docs.text:
Command Purpose MOVE Request movement STOP Stop commanded movement STATUS Request controller status POSITION Report position information SENSOR Report sensor measurements LIMIT Report an active limit switch FAULT Report a detected fault READY Indicate that a controller is ready

The final message format, baud rate, pin assignments, and error-checking method have not yet been finalized.

Back to Table of Contents

docs.title: Sensors and Indicators
docs.text: Our software will use several sensors and indicator lights.

docs.title: IR Receiver
docs.text:
The IR receiver will connect to Preston's Nano.

It will receive commands from a compatible TV remote and allow the user to control the robotic leg.

docs.title: Pressure Sensor
docs.text:
The pressure sensor will connect to Bex's Nano.

It will provide information about pressure or contact at the leg.

docs.title: IMU
docs.text:
The IMU will connect to Kaushik's Nano.

It will provide measurements related to motion and orientation.

docs.title: Limit Switches
docs.text:
Our current plan includes two limit switches for each joint.

Since the leg has three joints, this gives us six planned limit switches.

The switches will help prevent the joints from moving beyond their allowed range.

docs.title: Indicator Lights
docs.text:
LED Color Purpose Yellow Power indicator Green Board power indicator Blue Global status indicator White Joint status indicator

The exact software behavior for the blue and white indicators is still being determined.

Back to Table of Contents

docs.title: Safety and Fault Handling
docs.text: Our software will include checks to reduce the risk of uncontrolled movement and hardware damage.

docs.title: Joint Limits
docs.text:
Each joint controller will monitor its assigned limit switches.

When a travel limit is reached, the controller should prevent further movement in the restricted direction.

docs.title: Communication Loss
docs.text:
If a controller stops receiving valid communication for longer than an approved timeout, it should enter a safe state.

The exact timeout and stopping behavior will be selected and tested.

docs.title: Invalid Commands
docs.text:
Each controller should check incoming commands before operating its hardware.

Commands outside the allowed operating range should be rejected or limited.

docs.title: Fault Reporting
docs.text:
Possible faults include:

  • Communication loss
  • Invalid movement command
  • Joint limit reached
  • Sensor failure
  • Motor stall or overload
  • Position feedback failure

Each driver Nano should report detected faults to Preston's main controller.

Back to Table of Contents

docs.title: Software Testing Plan
docs.text: We plan to test each Nano individually before connecting the complete system.

docs.title: Individual Testing
docs.text: Controller Planned Tests Preston IR input, kinematics, and UART communication Akshan Servo control, limit switches, and feedback Bex Linear actuator control, pressure sensor, limit switches, and feedback Kaushik Linear actuator control, IMU, limit switches, and feedback

docs.title: Communication Testing
docs.text:
After individual testing, we will verify that:

  1. Commands are received correctly.
  2. Each Nano responds to the correct command.
  3. Sensor information is returned to the main Nano.
  4. Invalid commands are handled correctly.
  5. Communication loss causes the expected safe behavior.

docs.title: Full System Testing
docs.text:
Once the individual subsystems are working, we will combine all four Nanos.

We will test the complete process from receiving an IR remote command to calculating joint positions, moving the actuators, and receiving feedback.

We will also verify the limit switches, indicator lights, and fault handling.

These tests are planned and have not yet been reported as completed.

Back to Table of Contents

docs.title: Future Work
docs.text:
Our next steps are:

  1. Finalize the servo and linear actuator models.
  2. Select the motor drivers.
  3. Confirm the pressure sensor and IMU models.
  4. Finalize UART pin assignments.
  5. Define the UART message format.
  6. Complete the electrical schematics.
  7. Finalize the diagnostic display.
  8. Develop and test each Nano's software.
  9. Combine the four controllers.
  10. Test the complete robotic leg.

Our goal is to create a working software system where each Nano can perform its assigned task while communicating with the main controller.

docs.title: Who participated
docs.text: The ideation effort was completed by the full project team working together on the modular robotic leg design. Team members contributed ideas across multiple technical areas, including mechanical architecture, actuation, sensing, control, and end-effector design. The process was collaborative and based on group discussion rather than individual isolated design work.

docs.title: How the team met
docs.text: The team met regularly during the concept development phase to discuss the project direction and generate design ideas. Meetings were used to review the project goals, define design constraints, and evaluate new concepts as they emerged. The team also used these sessions to compare alternative approaches and refine promising features before finalizing the concepts.

docs.title: How ideas were collected
docs.text: Ideas were collected through structured team brainstorming sessions. Each member contributed design options for the leg architecture, actuation strategy, sensing approach, and interaction with the ground. Features were recorded as individual concepts, then discussed as a group to clarify purpose, feasibility, and relevance to the project. This ensured that the design space remained broad before concepts were narrowed down.

docs.title: Which project requirements were used
docs.text:
The brainstorming and ranking process was guided by the project requirements developed for the robotic leg system. The team used the needs and constraints from the project specification, including:

  • functional mobility and locomotion capability
  • feasible mechanical design for a six-legged robot
  • realistic actuation and power requirements
  • sensing and control suitability
  • manufacturability and modularity
  • safety and robustness
  • compatibility with the overall robot platform and use case

These requirements acted as the selection criteria for deciding which features were worth pursuing in more detail.

docs.title: Additional resources used during ideation
docs.text:
During ideation, the team used several supporting resources to expand and evaluate possible design directions. These included:

  • prior project research on walking robots and legged locomotion
  • benchmarking of existing robotic leg and hexapod systems
  • literature and examples from modular robotics and actuator design
  • design discussion informed by course project requirements and team goals
  • sketches, concept diagrams, and comparison notes generated during meetings

These resources helped the team ground the brainstorming process in practical engineering considerations while still encouraging creative exploration.

docs.title: How the features were grouped
docs.text:
After the initial list of ideas was generated, similar concepts were grouped into categories based on their function. Features were organized by design area, such as:

  • joint architecture and kinematics
  • rotary and linear actuation
  • feedback and sensing
  • ground interaction and foot design
  • modularity and maintainability
  • structure and manufacturing
  • safety and control

Grouping the features allowed the team to identify common design themes and avoid evaluating isolated ideas without context. This also made it easier to combine complementary ideas into complete product concepts.

docs.title: How rankings were assigned
docs.text:
The team assigned rankings by evaluating each feature against the project requirements and overall system value. Features were judged based on criteria such as:

  • how directly they supported the robot’s movement and stability
  • whether they improved performance or controllability
  • their manufacturability and integration difficulty
  • safety and reliability
  • modularity and future flexibility
  • expected usefulness for the selected concept direction

Features that best matched the project goals and seemed most feasible were ranked highest. The highest-ranked ideas were then recombined into the three product concepts that were developed and compared later in the design process.
